opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a widespread misconception right now, fueled by all the excitement around large language models, that robots are just a year or two away from doing everything humans can do with their hands. And I understand why people think that. We've seen these extraordinary leaps in language and image generation, and there are these very slick videos of humanoid robots doing backflips or folding a shirt. But I'd encourage people to be skeptical, because the physical world is fundamentally harder than the world of text.

Part of it is what we call Moravec's paradox, which is the observation that the things that are hard for humans, like playing chess or doing calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, while the things that are easy for us, like picking up a glass of water or cracking an egg, turn out to be incredibly hard for robots. We take for granted this enormous sensorimotor skill that we've evolved over millions of years. A child can walk into a kitchen and pick up objects they've never seen before. Robots still struggle with that.

Now think about a kitchen specifically. You've got objects of all different shapes, sizes, and textures. Things are wet, slippery, deformable. A tomato is different from a potato, and every tomato is a little different from the last one. You've got heat, steam, sharp knives, liquids sloshing around. A good line cook is constantly adjusting by feel: how firm is this, how much resistance am I getting from this cut, is the sauce thickening. Robots have very limited tactile sensing compared to human hands. Our fingertips are extraordinarily sensitive, and we have this rich feedback loop that we're barely aware of.

And then there's the data problem, which I think is underappreciated. Language models were trained on essentially the entire internet, billions and billions of examples. For robot manipulation, we don't have anything close to that. There's no internet-scale dataset of robot hands interacting with the world. People are trying to collect it, through teleoperation and simulation and learning from videos of humans, but I've estimated the gap is something like a hundred thousand years of data compared to what went into training these language models. Simulation helps, but simulating contact, friction, and deformable materials accurately is notoriously difficult. There's always a gap between simulation and reality.

Skilled trades like plumbing or electrical work have all those challenges plus more. Every job site is different. You're crawling under a sink in an old house where the pipes were installed fifty years ago and nothing is standard. You have to diagnose the problem, improvise, deal with corrosion and awkward angles and unexpected situations. That combination of dexterity, adaptability, and judgment in unstructured environments is exactly where robots are weakest.

So my advice to young people, and I say this to my own students, is that these trades are not going away anytime soon. I'm not saying never. I'm optimistic about progress, and I think we'll see robots helping in more structured settings like warehouses, where we already see a lot of success with bin picking. But I think the human touch, quite literally, is going to remain valuable for a long time. And frankly, I think that's good news. We should be thinking about robots as collaborators that make people's work easier and safer, rather than as replacements.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've been working on robot grasping and manipulation for a very long time now, and I'll tell you, the thing that still humbles me is what I'd call Moravec's paradox. The things that are hard for humans — playing chess, solving equations, even writing a decent essay — turned out to be relatively easy for machines. And the things that are trivially easy for a four-year-old, like picking up a cup, cracking an egg, folding a towel, those remain remarkably hard for robots.

A kitchen is really the perfect example of why. Think about what a line cook is doing. They're handling objects that are deformable, slippery, wet, hot, that change shape as you work with them. You're deboning a chicken, you're kneading dough, you're reaching into a cluttered drawer for a spatula without looking. Every one of those involves perception under uncertainty, contact physics that we really can't model precisely, and tactile feedback that our sensors are nowhere near matching. Human skin has thousands of receptors in the fingertips alone. We just don't have an equivalent yet.

And then there's the environment. Kitchens are unstructured, they're crowded, things get moved around, the lighting changes, there's steam, there's grease. Factories work for robots because we engineered the world around the robot. Everything is fixtured, everything arrives in the same position. A kitchen, or a construction site, or a plumbing job under someone's sink, is the exact opposite of that. Every house is different. Every pipe has been installed slightly wrong by somebody fifty years ago.

So with the skilled trades, the electrician, the plumber, the carpenter, you've got this combination of dexterity, improvisation, and judgment all in one. The plumber shows up and the problem is never quite what was described on the phone. They have to diagnose it, adapt, crawl into an awkward space, apply just the right amount of force. We're seeing wonderful progress in learning-based approaches, and I don't want to dismiss that. But the data problem is severe. Language models had the whole internet to train on. There's no internet of physical manipulation experience. Every grasp a robot learns, somebody has to go collect that data, and the long tail of situations is enormous.

So my honest view is that these jobs are going to be among the last to be automated, not the first. I think that's actually a somewhat counterintuitive message, because people assumed the blue-collar work would go first and the knowledge work would be safe. In many ways it's turning out to be the reverse.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we tend to underestimate how much intelligence is involved in working with your hands. In a kitchen, you’re dealing with objects that vary enormously. A tomato can be firm or soft, slippery or bruised. As you cut it, you’re constantly adjusting based on what you see and feel. You don’t usually think of that as a difficult computation, but for a robot it’s a very demanding problem.

And it’s not enough to get it right once. A robot has to handle all those variations reliably, and recover when something goes wrong. If an ingredient slips out of your grasp, a person can usually improvise. For a robot, that can interrupt the whole task.

The same applies to plumbing or electrical work. You’re often working in a space you’ve never seen before, with limited access, and things aren’t quite where you expected them to be. You have to diagnose the situation and adapt your movements together.

So there will be individual tasks we can automate, especially if we can arrange the environment to make them easier. But the flexibility of a skilled person—to walk into an unfamiliar kitchen or worksite and just figure out what to do—is a much higher bar.

r001.rationale: The response says food items such as tomatoes vary in firmness and condition, requiring continual adjustments that make robotic handling difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we tend to underestimate how much intelligence is involved in working with your hands. In a kitchen, you’re dealing with objects that are deformable, slippery, and different every time. Two tomatoes don’t behave exactly the same way. And as you cut something or cook it, its properties change. You have to keep sensing what’s happening and adjusting.

A factory is much easier to structure. You can arrange for a part to arrive in a known position, and you can design a gripper specifically for that part. In a kitchen, or if you’re a plumber working under somebody’s sink, you don’t have that luxury. You encounter something unexpected, you have limited visibility, and you have to figure out how much force to apply without breaking anything.

Humans make those adjustments so naturally that we hardly notice them. But getting a robot to perceive the situation, choose an action, and recover when that action doesn’t work is very difficult. We can automate particular steps. The challenge is getting the flexibility and reliability you need to do the whole job.

r001.rationale: It says that two tomatoes do not behave exactly the same, identifying variation between individual food items as a challenge for kitchen automation.
